Before you commit Whose dividing fence is it, and who pays for what A fence built on the actual boundary line is legally a dividing fence, not just a shared one, and Queensland's Neighbourhood Disputes (Dividing Fences and Trees) Act 2011 sets a formula for splitting the bill. Both owners are generally on the hook equally, but only up to a sufficient dividing fence - broadly 0.5 m to 1.8 m high, built from a prescribed material like palings, chain wire, metal panels or brick. Want a taller run, a premium finish, or Colorbond over something cheaper? That upgrade is on your bill alone, which is the part that catches most people out. A short conversation next door, backed by a written quote, settles this more often than not. When it doesn't, the formal route is a notice to contribute : an approved form setting out the land, the fence line, the scope of work and an estimated cost, with a written quote attached. No agreement inside a month, and either owner can take it to QCAT within the following two months. Splitting the invoice so each household pays its own share keeps you out of that chase entirely - though nobody, us included, can promise how a neighbour will actually respond. General information as at July 2026. The current rules are published by the Queensland Government and dividing-fence disputes are heard by QCAT . Three rules worth knowing before you order Height: stay at or under 2 m above natural ground and Queensland treats the fence as accepted development. Cross 2 m and a certifier has to sign off first - and a fence sitting on top of a retaining wall counts the wall in that measurement, so a modest wall plus a standard fence can tip over the line without anyone meaning to. Corners: intersections carry sight-line rules, so front fencing on a corner block stays low enough that a driver can actually see who's coming. Pools: a pool barrier answers to its own standard entirely, and only a licensed pool safety inspector can sign it off - not a fencer, and not a checklist.
